 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the pooled reference values, such as blood lactate above 10 mmol/L, as targets for every RST session, when they are averages across many protocols, sports and athlete types.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2023,
   "citation":"Thurlow F, Weakley J, Townshend AD, Timmins RG, Morrison M, McLaren SJ. The Acute Demands of Repeated-Sprint Training on Physiological, Neuromuscular, Perceptual and Performance Outcomes in Team Sport Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2023.",
   "doi":"10.1007/s40279-023-01853-w",
   "abstract":"Systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of 176 studies (908 samples) of overground repeated-sprint training in team sport athletes aged 16 or over. Pooled reference estimates were 163 bpm average heart rate, 10.7 mmol/L end-set blood lactate and 5.0% sprint decrement. Shuttle-based sprints, longer sprint distances and shorter inter-repetition rest increased or altered physiological and performance demands, while two fewer repetitions per set had a trivial effect on most outcomes.",
   "tldr":"Repeated-sprint training is physically demanding for team sport athletes, with pooled blood lactate of about 10.7 mmol/L. Longer sprints and shorter rest raise the demand, while dropping from six to four repetitions per set changed most outcomes very little.",
   "methods":"PRISMA-guided systematic search of PubMed, SPORTDiscus, MEDLINE and Scopus (to January 2022) for original studies of overground running repeated-sprint training in team sport athletes aged 16 or over. Data were pooled with multilevel mixed-effects meta-analysis, and programming moderators (sprint modality, repetitions per set, sprint distance, rest modality and rest duration) were tested by meta-regression against a reference of 6 x 30 m straight sprints with 20 s passive rest. Effects were judged against practical thresholds as trivial, substantial or inconclusive.",
   "findings":"Pooled reference estimates were average heart rate 163 bpm (90% CI 154 to 171), peak heart rate 182 bpm, end-set blood lactate 10.7 mmol/L, session RPE 6.5 deciMax, best sprint time 5.52 s and sprint decrement 5.0% (90% CI 4.7 to 5.3). Shuttle-based sprints increased average and best sprint times (1.42 s and 1.55 s slower) with a trivial effect on session RPE. Two more repetitions per set had trivial effects on most outcomes. A 10 m longer sprint increased blood lactate by 2.7 mmol/L and sprint decrement by 1.7%. A 10 s longer rest lowered blood lactate by 1.1 mmol/L and sprint decrement by 1.4%, with trivial effects on peak heart rate and session RPE. Active rest and rest modality effects were largely inconclusive.",
   "limitations":"Meta-analysis could only be run where enough samples existed, so VO2, creatine kinase, CMJ height and peak heart rate as a percentage of maximum were not pooled or moderated. Data from some studies were not supplied by the authors and were estimated, and the review excluded injured athletes and sprints in hot conditions.",

To limit fatigue and protect sprint times, shorter sprints (15 to 25 m) with 30 s or more passive rest are suggested. Reducing from six to four repetitions per set changed most measured demands only trivially, so it may cut sprint volume without much loss of stimulus on average.",

                                                               professional football players. International Journal of Sports Medicine 2024. doi: 10.1055/a-2282-0024




                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
                                                               Conflict of Interest: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest.

                                                               Abstract:
                                                               The purpose of this study was to analyse the association and predictive capacity between the acute:chronic workload ratio




                                                                                                                                                                            
----
                                                                                                 Article

The anabolic response to protein ingestion during
recovery from exercise has no upper limit in
magnitude and duration in vivo in humans
Graphical abstract                                                   Authors
                                                                     Jorn Trommelen, Glenn A.A. van Lieshout,
                                                                     Jean Nyakayiru, ..., Joy P.B. Goessens,
                                                                     Annemie P. Gijsen, Luc J.C. van Loon

                                                                     Correspondence
                                                                     l.vanloon@maastrichtuniversity.nl

                                                                     In brief
                                                                     Trommelen et al. investigate the anabolic
                                                                     response to the ingestion of various
                                                                     amounts of protein following exercise and
                                                                     demonstrate a dose-response increase in
                                                                     the magnitude and duration of protein
                                                                     absorption, muscle protein synthesis
                                                                     rates, and whole-body net protein
                                                                     balance. The anabolic response to
                                                                     protein ingestion has no upper limit.




Highlights
d   Postprandial protein anabolism remains elevated during
    prolonged hyperaminoacidemia

d   Protein ingestion has a negligible impact on whole-body
    amino acid oxidation

d   Muscle protein autophagy is not modulated by protein
    ingestion

d   Exogenous amino acids are the main precursors in
    postprandial protein accretion




           Trommelen et al., 2023, Cell Reports Medicine 4, 101324
           December 19, 2023 ª 2023 The Author(s).
           https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xcrm.2023.101324                                               ll

119	
120	                                                               23        Currently, one of the main objectives of physical preparation in any type of sport is to

126	
127	                                                               27sports like football [2], which is a major problem for clubs in both sporting and economic

                                                               Abstract:
                                                               The purpose of this study was to analyse the association and predictive capacity between the acute:chronic workload ratio




                                                                                                                                                                                                         Accepted Manuscript
                                                               (ACWR) and non-contact injuries in a semiprofessional football team. 17 football players from a Spanish Third Division foot-
                                                               ball team participated voluntarily in this study. A prospective longitudinal study was developed during 2020/2021 season. 24
                                                               weeks were analysed from October to March, including a regenerative microcycle due to the absence of competition during
                                                               Christmas. Ratio perceived exertion (RPE) and session- ratio perceived exertion (sRPE) were registered for every training and
                                                               game session. After that, acute and chronic workloads were calculated, as well as ACWR was derived from them. Furthermore,
                                                               non-contact injuries were registered during the mentioned period. The main findings were: there is no significant association
                                                               between the ACWR and non-contact injuries (0.069 (p<0.05)) and, the use of the ACWR by itself is insufficient to predict the
                                                               occurrence of non-contact injuries in a semiprofessional football team. Consequently, the ACWR is not an useful predictive tool
                                                               for injuries in semiprofessional football teams.

                                                               22Introduction

                                                               23        Currently, one of the main objectives of physical preparation in any type of sport is to

                                                               24promote the full availability and well-being of players to the greatest extent possible and thus
                                                                25reduce the risk of injury [1]. However, despite the efforts carried out to meet this objective in

                                                               26both human and material terms, a high number of injuries are recorded each year in team

                                                               27sports like football [2], which is a major problem for clubs in both sporting and economic

                                                               28terms. In football nowadays, although the injury rate is going down [3], the total number of

                                                               29specific types of injuries, such as hamstring injuries, has actually increased in recent years [4].

                                                               30In any case, the reality is that having fewer injuries during the season is related to greater

                                                               31sporting success [5, 6], so clubs should strive to meet this objective.




This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
                                                               32        Faced with this issue, science provides a range of tools with a solid scientific backing

                                                               33which have proved to be effective in minimizing both the appearance and severity of injuries.




                                                                                                                                                                                    Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
                                                               34Different tools can be applied in different football contexts in order to reduce the number and

                                                               35severity of injuries. Some of the means that can be relied on to achieve these objectives




                                                                                                                                                                       Accepted Manuscript
                                                               36include the following: workload control using GPS [7, 8], the use of assessment tests [9],

                                                               37warm-up/activation protocols [10] or other recovery strategies [11].

                                                               38        Quantification of training load and injury prevention require both human and material

                                                               39resources and sometimes such costs are unaffordable for many clubs, due to economic

                                                               40limitations. In this sense, there are alternatives that can help in the search for solutions. The

                                                               41Subjective Perception of Effort [SPE] [12] is a tool for quantifying the training workload

                                                               42without any economic cost and is applicable in non-professional contexts which can facilitate

                                                               43the quantification of the training workload without the need for significant resources [13].

                                                               44Despite being a subjective tool, it has been validated in recent decades due to its high

                                                               45correlation with different internal workload variables, such as heart rate or oxygen

                                                               46consumption [13, 14]. In addition, it is also valid for external workload measures such as total

                                                               47distance travelled or player workload [14, 15].

                                                               48        In this way, the acute:chronic workload ratio [ACWR] is purported to predict injury

                                                               49risk. It yields a training workload value and the player increases or decreases his/her chances
                                                                50of getting injured depending on that value [16]. This model considers the risk that an athlete

                                                               51has of getting injured, based on the relationship between their current state of fitness (chronic

                                                               52workload) and their level of fatigue (acute workload) [16]. According to Gabbett [16], as long

                                                               53as said ratio remains between a value of 0.8 and 1.3, the player is considered to be within the

                                                               54"sweet spot", i.e. having an optimal ACWR to minimize the potential risk of injury. On the

                                                               55other hand, when the ratio exceeds 1.5 or falls below 0.8, the player enters the "red zone" and

                                                               56the risk of suffering an injury increases.

495	                                                               178Discussion
496	
497	                                                               179        To date, this is the first ever study to verify the association and predictive capacity of
498	
499	                                                               180the ACWR with the risk of injury in semiprofessional football players. The objective of this
500	
501	
502	
503	
504	This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
505	                                                               181study was to analyse the association and predictive capacity between the ACWR workload
506	
507	                                                               182ratio and non-contact injuries in a semiprofessional football team. In relation to this, the main
508	
509	
510	
511	
512	                                                                                                                                                                                    Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
513	                                                               183findings were: a) there is no significant association between the ACWR and non-contact
514	
515	                                                               184injuries and b) the use of the ACWR by itself is insufficient to predict the occurrence of non-
516	
517	
518	
519	
520	                                                                                                                                                                       Accepted Manuscript
521	                                                               185contact injuries in a semiprofessional football team.
522	
523	                                                               186        The team studied had an injury incidence of 8.86 injuries per 1000 hours of practice
524	
525	                                                               187during the analysed season (Table 2). This value is very close to the one presented by
526	
527	                                                               188Beijsterveldt et al. [33], who obtained an injury incidence of 9.6 in amateur football players.
528	
529	                                                               189However, there are other non-professional environments studied which have reported
530	
531	                                                               190significantly lower incidences. For example, Hägglund et al. [34] found an incidence among
532	
533	                                                               191their football players of 5.2 injuries per thousand hours of practice. Regarding the types of
534	
535	                                                               192injuries suffered, Beijsterveldt et al. [33] and Hägglund et al. [34] reported 23.6% and 14.3%
536	
537	                                                               193of ligamentous injuries respectively, which are values similar to the 20% of this particular
538	
539	                                                               194type of injury obtained in the present study. In addition, muscular injuries at 70%, and tendon
540	
541	                                                               195injuries at 10% vary meaningfully from the percentages found by these authors for these types
542	
543	                                                               196of injuries: 48.4% muscular, 43.8% tendon [34] and 38.9% muscle-tendon [33]. These
544	
545	                                                               197differences are probably due to the fact that the time period studied in these works was longer
546	
547	                                                               198than the period analysed in the present research, which suggests that if a longer follow-up
548	                                                                199were carried out, the percentage of each type of injury obtained would possibly be similar to a
549	
550	                                                               200large degree.
551	
552	                                                               201        In order to respond to the main objective of the study, the sensitivity of the test was
553	
554	                                                               202obtained, which is defined as the ability of a test to detect a positive when the subject is
555	
556	                                                               203positive [i.e. true positive] and the specificity of the test, which is defined as the ability of a
557	
558	                                                               204test to detect a negative when the subject is negative (i.e. true negative) [32]. The sensitivity
559	
560	                                                               205and specificity (see Table 4) obtained were 50.00% and 31.35% respectively, which are
561	
562	
563	
564	
565	This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
566	                                                               206results that show low predictive capacity when detecting non-contact injuries using the
567	
568	                                                               207ACWR as a predictor. This result supports the conclusion of Fanchini et al. [22], who state
569	
570	
571	
572	
573	                                                                                                                                                                                     Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
574	                                                               208that this tool has a poor predictive ability when it comes to detecting future non-contact
575	
576	                                                               209injuries in football players. They found a sensitivity of 20.0% which opposes the one shown
577	
578	
579	
580	
581	                                                                                                                                                                        Accepted Manuscript
582	                                                               210by Gabbett [16], who obtained a sensitivity of 87.1% and a specificity of 98.8%.
583	
584	                                                               211        On the other hand, in relation to the association between the ACWR and the risk of
585	
586	                                                               212non-contact injury, Fanchini et al. [22] found that the ACWR is positively related to a higher
587	
588	                                                               213risk of injury, that is, the higher the ACWR, the greater the risk of getting a non-contact
589	
590	                                                               214injury. The correlation test applied in the present study (see table 3) shows that there is no
591	
592	                                                               215relationship between the ACWR and the occurrence of injuries. However, once again the
593	
594	                                                               216shorter time period studied may be one of the reasons why such a relationship does not
595	
596	                                                               217appear, since the total number of non-contact injuries suffered is lower [n=10] than, for
597	
598	                                                               218example, in the study by Fanchini et al. (n=90) [22], or in Gabbet´s study (n=139) [16].
599	
600	                                                               219        In any case, the results show that the predictive capacity of the ACWR is weak, which
601	
602	                                                               220is in line with one section of the scientific community [21–24], who currently strongly rejects
603	
604	                                                               221this idea, arguing that the values of the ratio are based on erroneous conceptual premises [24],
605	
606	                                                               222both from a mathematical and practical point of view, concluding that the recommendations
607	
608	                                                               223on its use within team planning must be updated and corrected in order to avoid its use [21].
609	                                                                224        Despite the fact that the present investigation has found a weak relationship between
610	
611	                                                               225the ACWR and the occurrence of injuries (table 3), in addition to poor predictive capacity to
612	
613	                                                               226detect future injuries (table 4), other studies have been able to associate both variables. Said
614	
615	                                                               227studies find, for instance, that an ACWR between 1.00 and 1.25 reduces the risk of suffering a
616	
617	                                                               228non-contact injury [18], that ACWR ≥1.5 increase the probability of non-contact injury [16,
618	
619	                                                               22918] and that large spikes in acute workload or sudden increases in workload correspond to an
620	
621	                                                               230increased risk of non-contact injury [19]. In spite of these findings, and as pointed out by
622	
623	
624	
625	
626	This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
627	                                                               231Griffin et al. [23], the fact that there is an association between the ACWR and non-contact
628	
629	                                                               232injuries does not mean that these can be predicted using this method, since the relationship
630	
631	
632	
633	
634	                                                                                                                                                                                   Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
635	                                                               233and the predictive ability are two different things.
636	
637	                                                               234        However, although no association has been found between the ACWR and the risk of
638	
639	
640	
641	
642	                                                                                                                                                                      Accepted Manuscript
643	                                                               235non-contact injury, in recent years recent studies have shown how the weekly organization of
644	
645	                                                               236the load influences the risk of injury, especially in periods of high competitive congestion
646	
647	                                                               237[35–37], so targeting the use of the ACWR to this goal may be useful since, when football
648	
649	                                                               238players suffer non-contact injuries, such as anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) or common
650	
651	                                                               239muscle injuries in football like hamstring muscle injuries, several risk factors environmental,
652	
653	                                                               240anatomical, hormonal, neuromuscular, biomechanical, hours of exposure (both train and
654	
655	                                                               241match) are known that predispose the athlete to having a greater or lesser risk of getting them
656	
657	                                                               242[38–41]. Technical staff works on such areas so as to try to eliminate them or, at least, reduce
658	
659	                                                               243their presence to the greatest extent possible in each of the players. Some of these risk factors
660	
661	                                                               244are related to the training workload, which can lead to a greater or lesser risk of getting an
662	
663	                                                               245injury depending on how it is administered [42]. It is at this point when the ACWR can be
664	
665	                                                               246used as a tool in injury prevention, since it enables regulation of the training workload
666	
667	                                                               247received by each of the athletes.
668	                                                                248        In view of the above, the idea that the ACWR is a good predictor of the risk of getting
669	
670	                                                               249injured is ruled out since it has been proven to be an ineffective predictor on its own when
671	
672	                                                               250detecting the occurrence of non-contact injuries in semiprofessional football players.
673	
674	                                                               251However, the control of the training workload through the use of sRPE and obtaining the
675	
676	                                                               252ACWR has been defined as a risk factor when football players get a non-contact injury [43].
677	
678	                                                               253Therefore, the control of said risk factor by technical staff may be an option so as to try to
679	
680	                                                               254reduce the number of injuries suffered. Consequently, the control of such risk factor by the
681	
682	
683	
684	
685	This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
686	                                                               255coaching staff may be an option to try to reduce the number of injuries suffered, especially in
687	
688	                                                               256semiprofessional environments where the use of a free tool, such as the sRPE is a point in
689	
690	
691	
692	
693	                                                                                                                                                                                 Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
694	                                                               257favour of its use since the economic possibilities of this type of club are lower than those of
695	
696	                                                               258professional clubs and they cannot afford more expensive technologies such as GPS.
697	
698	
699	
700	
701	                                                                                                                                                                    Accepted Manuscript
702	                                                               259        The main limitation of the study is that the number of injuries registered was low,
703	
704	                                                               260especially if we compared with similar studies that analysed this topic. This makes that our
705	
706	                                                               261conclusions should be taken with caution. In addition, the sample size was small, with only a
707	
708	                                                               262team. However, most of studies in this topic also reported the ACWR analysis with only one
709	
710	                                                               263team, in different TIER levels. Regarding this, the semiprofessional nature of the team
711	
712	                                                               264allowed the development of other sports activities outside training and match hours, and the
713	
714	                                                               265daily work of each player could be more or less physically demanding, which may or may not
715	
716	                                                               266have influenced their workload and fatigue levels.
717	
718	
719	                                                               267Conclusion
720	
721	                                                               268        The aim of this study was to analyse the association and predictive capacity between
722	
723	                                                               269the ACWR workload ratio and non-contact injuries in a semiprofessional football team. The
724	
725	                                                               270results reject the idea that the value of the ACWR is correlated with the risk of non-contact
726	
727	                                                               271injuries. Similarly, nothing has been found to support the ability to predict the occurrence of
728	
729	                                                               272non-contact injuries using the ACWR workload ratio, perhaps because injuries are
730	                                                                273multifactorial (hormonal, neuromuscular, uncontrollable factors...) and cannot be reduced to a
731	
732	                                                               274single factor.
733	
734	                                                               275        In any case, the use of this tool in team planning and players management does not
735	
736	                                                               276seem to be suitable as an injury prediction tool. Thus, other training load monitoring strategies
737	
738	                                                               277are recommended to control and modulate the training process in team sports.

                                                                                                                                                                                    Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
                                                               183findings were: a) there is no significant association between the ACWR and non-contact

                                                               184injuries and b) the use of the ACWR by itself is insufficient to predict the occurrence of non-




                                                                                                                                                                       Accepted Manuscript
                                                               185contact injuries in a semiprofessional football team.

                                                               186        The team studied had an injury incidence of 8.86 injuries per 1000 hours of practice

                                                               187during the analysed season (Table 2). This value is very close to the one presented by

                                                               188Beijsterveldt et al. [33], who obtained an injury incidence of 9.6 in amateur football players.

                                                               189However, there are other non-professional environments studied which have reported

                                                               190significantly lower incidences. For example, Hägglund et al. [34] found an incidence among

                                                               191their football players of 5.2 injuries per thousand hours of practice. Regarding the types of

                                                               192injuries suffered, Beijsterveldt et al. [33] and Hägglund et al. [34] reported 23.6% and 14.3%

                                                               193of ligamentous injuries respectively, which are values similar to the 20% of this particular

                                                               194type of injury obtained in the present study. In addition, muscular injuries at 70%, and tendon

                                                               195injuries at 10% vary meaningfully from the percentages found by these authors for these types

                                                               196of injuries: 48.4% muscular, 43.8% tendon [34] and 38.9% muscle-tendon [33]. These

                                                               197differences are probably due to the fact that the time period studied in these works was longer

                                                               198than the period analysed in the present research, which suggests that if a longer follow-up
                                                                199were carried out, the percentage of each type of injury obtained would possibly be similar to a

                                                               200large degree.

                                                               201        In order to respond to the main objective of the study, the sensitivity of the test was

                                                               202obtained, which is defined as the ability of a test to detect a positive when the subject is

                                                               203positive [i.e. true positive] and the specificity of the test, which is defined as the ability of a

                                                               204test to detect a negative when the subject is negative (i.e. true negative) [32]. The sensitivity

                                                               205and specificity (see Table 4) obtained were 50.00% and 31.35% respectively, which are




This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
                                                               206results that show low predictive capacity when detecting non-contact injuries using the

                                                               207ACWR as a predictor. This result supports the conclusion of Fanchini et al. [22], who state




                                                                                                                                                                                     Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
                                                               208that this tool has a poor predictive ability when it comes to detecting future non-contact

                                                               209injuries in football players. They found a sensitivity of 20.0% which opposes the one shown




                                                                                                                                                                        Accepted Manuscript
                                                               210by Gabbett [16], who obtained a sensitivity of 87.1% and a specificity of 98.8%.

                                                               211        On the other hand, in relation to the association between the ACWR and the risk of

                                                               212non-contact injury, Fanchini et al. [22] found that the ACWR is positively related to a higher

                                                               213risk of injury, that is, the higher the ACWR, the greater the risk of getting a non-contact

                                                               214injury. The correlation test applied in the present study (see table 3) shows that there is no

                                                               215relationship between the ACWR and the occurrence of injuries. However, once again the

                                                               216shorter time period studied may be one of the reasons why such a relationship does not

                                                               217appear, since the total number of non-contact injuries suffered is lower [n=10] than, for

                                                               218example, in the study by Fanchini et al. (n=90) [22], or in Gabbet´s study (n=139) [16].

                                                               219        In any case, the results show that the predictive capacity of the ACWR is weak, which

                                                               220is in line with one section of the scientific community [21–24], who currently strongly rejects

                                                               221this idea, arguing that the values of the ratio are based on erroneous conceptual premises [24],

                                                               222both from a mathematical and practical point of view, concluding that the recommendations

                                                               223on its use within team planning must be updated and corrected in order to avoid its use [21].
                                                                224        Despite the fact that the present investigation has found a weak relationship between

                                                               225the ACWR and the occurrence of injuries (table 3), in addition to poor predictive capacity to

                                                               226detect future injuries (table 4), other studies have been able to associate both variables. Said

                                                               227studies find, for instance, that an ACWR between 1.00 and 1.25 reduces the risk of suffering a

                                                               228non-contact injury [18], that ACWR ≥1.5 increase the probability of non-contact injury [16,

                                                               22918] and that large spikes in acute workload or sudden increases in workload correspond to an

                                                               230increased risk of non-contact injury [19]. In spite of these findings, and as pointed out by




This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
                                                               231Griffin et al. [23], the fact that there is an association between the ACWR and non-contact

                                                               232injuries does not mean that these can be predicted using this method, since the relationship




                                                                                                                                                                                   Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
                                                               233and the predictive ability are two different things.

                                                               234        However, although no association has been found between the ACWR and the risk of




                                                                                                                                                                      Accepted Manuscript
                                                               235non-contact injury, in recent years recent studies have shown how the weekly organization of

                                                               236the load influences the risk of injury, especially in periods of high competitive congestion

                                                               237[35–37], so targeting the use of the ACWR to this goal may be useful since, when football

                                                               238players suffer non-contact injuries, such as anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) or common

                                                               239muscle injuries in football like hamstring muscle injuries, several risk factors environmental,

                                                               240anatomical, hormonal, neuromuscular, biomechanical, hours of exposure (both train and

                                                               241match) are known that predispose the athlete to having a greater or lesser risk of getting them

                                                               242[38–41]. Technical staff works on such areas so as to try to eliminate them or, at least, reduce

                                                               243their presence to the greatest extent possible in each of the players. Some of these risk factors

                                                               244are related to the training workload, which can lead to a greater or lesser risk of getting an

                                                               245injury depending on how it is administered [42]. It is at this point when the ACWR can be

                                                               246used as a tool in injury prevention, since it enables regulation of the training workload

                                                               247received by each of the athletes.
                                                                248        In view of the above, the idea that the ACWR is a good predictor of the risk of getting

                                                               249injured is ruled out since it has been proven to be an ineffective predictor on its own when

                                                               250detecting the occurrence of non-contact injuries in semiprofessional football players.

                                                               251However, the control of the training workload through the use of sRPE and obtaining the

                                                               252ACWR has been defined as a risk factor when football players get a non-contact injury [43].

                                                               253Therefore, the control of said risk factor by technical staff may be an option so as to try to

                                                               254reduce the number of injuries suffered. Consequently, the control of such risk factor by the




This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
                                                               255coaching staff may be an option to try to reduce the number of injuries suffered, especially in

                                                               256semiprofessional environments where the use of a free tool, such as the sRPE is a point in




                                                                                                                                                                                 Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
                                                               257favour of its use since the economic possibilities of this type of club are lower than those of

                                                               258professional clubs and they cannot afford more expensive technologies such as GPS.




                                                                                                                                                                    Accepted Manuscript
                                                               259        The main limitation of the study is that the number of injuries registered was low,

                                                               260especially if we compared with similar studies that analysed this topic. This makes that our

                                                               261conclusions should be taken with caution. In addition, the sample size was small, with only a

                                                               262team. However, most of studies in this topic also reported the ACWR analysis with only one

                                                               263team, in different TIER levels. Regarding this, the semiprofessional nature of the team

                                                               264allowed the development of other sports activities outside training and match hours, and the

                                                               265daily work of each player could be more or less physically demanding, which may or may not

                                                               266have influenced their workload and fatigue levels.


                                                               267Conclusion

                                                               268        The aim of this study was to analyse the association and predictive capacity between

                                                               269the ACWR workload ratio and non-contact injuries in a semiprofessional football team. The

                                                               270results reject the idea that the value of the ACWR is correlated with the risk of non-contact

                                                               271injuries. Similarly, nothing has been found to support the ability to predict the occurrence of

                                                               272non-contact injuries using the ACWR workload ratio, perhaps because injuries are
                                                                273multifactorial (hormonal, neuromuscular, uncontrollable factors...) and cannot be reduced to a

                                                               274single factor.

                                                               275        In any case, the use of this tool in team planning and players management does not

                                                               276seem to be suitable as an injury prediction tool. Thus, other training load monitoring strategies

                                                               277are recommended to control and modulate the training process in team sports.

 "evidenceSummary":"A prospective observational study of 17 outfield players from one Spanish Third Division (semiprofessional) team, tracked over 24 weeks of the 2020/21 season. Session RPE and an exponentially weighted acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) were compared with 10 non-contact time-loss injuries (5.91 per 1,000 hours). Spearman rho between ACWR and non-contact injury was 0.069 (N = 2,565 observations), and 5 of the 10 injuries occurred with an ACWR outside 0.8 to 1.5, which the authors conclude is insufficient for prediction.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only 10 non-contact injuries from a single squad of 17 players means the sensitivity and predictive estimates are very imprecise. The specificity reported in Table 4 (31.35%) equals the false-positive rate (801 of 2,555), so the specificity from the same table is 68.7%, not the figure quoted.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the 0.8 to 1.5 ACWR band as a reliable injury alarm, when this study found the ACWR alone did not predict non-contact injuries.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Seco-Serna R, Lago-Fuentes C, Barcala-Furelos M. The acute:chronic workload ratio and injury risk in semiprofessional football players. Int J Sports Med. 2024. Accepted manuscript.",
   "doi":"10.1055/a-2282-0024",
   "abstract":"Prospective longitudinal study of 17 outfield players from a Spanish Third Division team over 24 weeks of the 2020/21 season, comparing session-RPE acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) with non-contact injuries. The authors found no meaningful association (rho = 0.069) and concluded that the ACWR alone is insufficient to predict non-contact injury in semiprofessional football.",
   "tldr":"In one semiprofessional squad, a session-RPE acute:chronic workload ratio did not predict non-contact injuries, and it flagged only 5 of the 10 that occurred. The authors conclude the ratio should not be used as a stand-alone injury tool, while cheap session-RPE load tracking may still be useful.",
   "methods":"Prospective observational study during the 2020/21 season in 17 outfield players, with data across 24 weeks (October to March). Session RPE (modified Borg scale) was recorded after every training session and match, and the EWMA ACWR was calculated with 7-day acute and 28-day chronic windows. Time-loss non-contact injuries were logged, and players were excluded from analysis while injured. Association was tested with Spearman correlation, and a 2x2 analysis classed an ACWR of 1.5 or above, or below 0.8, as a positive result.",
   "findings":"Ten non-contact injuries occurred, 70% of them muscular, with an incidence of 5.91 per 1,000 hours and a mean of 11.9 days out. The Spearman correlation between ACWR and non-contact injury was 0.069 (N = 2,565), reported as very low. Five injuries occurred with an ACWR of 1.5 or above, or below 0.8, giving a sensitivity of 50%. The authors report specificity of 31.35%.",
   "limitations":"Only 10 non-contact injuries (5 flagged by the ACWR) from one squad, so the estimates are imprecise. The abstract and discussion call the association non-significant, but Table 3 marks rho = 0.069 as p < 0.05, and Table 3 treats repeated player-day observations as independent. The 31.35% specificity equals the false-positive rate (801 of 2,555); the specificity from Table 4 is 68.7%, so that figure is misreported.",
   "practicalImplications":"Session RPE is a low-cost load measure that clubs without GPS can collect, but this study found that the ACWR alone did not identify which players would suffer non-contact injuries. Treat the ACWR as one part of load monitoring, not a stand-alone injury alarm, and use other monitoring strategies as the authors recommend.",
   "athleteDev":"Session-RPE load tracking is feasible in a semiprofessional squad without GPS. The study did not test whether ACWR-guided changes to training improve performance, so this use remains untested.",
   "rtp":"The study did not evaluate the ACWR as a guide to return to play. Injured players were removed from analysis until they returned to full training, so the findings cannot be used to judge readiness after injury."
 }
}

SUMMARY

The belief that the anabolic response to feeding during postexercise recovery is transient and has an upper
limit and that excess amino acids are being oxidized lacks scientific proof. Using a comprehensive quadruple
isotope tracer feeding-infusion approach, we show that the ingestion of 100 g protein results in a greater and
more prolonged (>12 h) anabolic response when compared to the ingestion of 25 g protein. We demonstrate a
dose-response increase in dietary-protein-derived plasma amino acid availability and subsequent incorpo-
ration into muscle protein. Ingestion of a large bolus of protein further increases whole-body protein net bal-
ance, mixed-muscle, myofibrillar, muscle connective, and plasma protein synthesis rates. Protein ingestion
has a negligible impact on whole-body protein breakdown rates or amino acid oxidation rates. These findings
demonstrate that the magnitude and duration of the anabolic response to protein ingestion is not restricted
and has previously been underestimated in vivo in humans.

content.content:
A total of 36 healthy, recreationally active young men were selected to participate in this parallel group, randomized double blind
placebo-controlled trial. Inclusion criteria were: male, aged between 18 and 40 years, healthy, and body mass index between
18.5 and 30 kg m2. Exclusion criteria were: smoking, sports/exercise <1 or >3 sessions per week, lactose intolerant, a history of
neuromuscular problems, use of anticoagulation medication, and individuals taking any medication known to affect protein meta-
bolism. Subject characteristics are presented in Table S1.

Pretesting
Participants underwent an initial screening session to assess height, weight, and body composition. Body composition was as-
sessed by bioelectric impedance (Star Test protocol, BioScan 920-2, Maltron International, Essex, UK). Participants were deemed
healthy based on their responses to a medical questionnaire and screening results. The subjects were then familiarized with the resis-
tance-type exercise protocol and the exercise equipment. All exercises during pretesting and experimental trials were supervised by
trained personnel. Subjects started by performing a 5-min cycling warm-up at 100 W before completing an estimation of their
1-repetition maximum (1-RM) on the leg press, leg extension, chest press, and lat pulldown exercises using the multiple repetitions
testing procedure.55 For each exercise, subjects performed 10 submaximal repetitions to become familiarized with the equipment
and to have lifting technique critiqued and properly adjusted. Sets were then performed at progressively increasing loads until failure
to perform a valid estimation within 3–6 repetitions of the set. A repetition was valid if the subject was able to complete the entire lift in
a controlled manner without assistance. A 2-min resting period between subsequent attempts was allowed. The pretesting and
experimental trials were separated by at least 7 days.

Diet and physical activity
All subjects were instructed to refrain from exhaustive physical labor and exercise and to keep their diet as constant as possible
Participants were randomly assigned to ingest a beverage containing 800 mL water with either 0 g, 25 g, or 100 g intrinsically L-
[1-13C]-phenylalanine and L-[1-13C]-leucine labeled milk protein (described below). Randomization was performed using a comput-
erized list randomizer (http://www.randomization.com/) and participants were sequentially allocated to a treatment according to the
randomized list. An independent person was responsible for random assignment (n = 12 per group) and preparation of the study
treatment beverages, which were sequentially numbered according to subject number. The beverages were prepared in a nontrans-
parent plastic container and provided in a double-blind fashion.

Production of intrinsically labeled milk protein

 "evidenceSummary":"A double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial in 36 healthy, recreationally active young men (12 per group) who ingested 0, 25 or 100 g of intrinsically labelled milk protein after one bout of whole-body resistance exercise, with sampling over 12 hours. The 100 g dose gave a greater and longer plasma amino acid response and higher muscle protein synthesis than 25 g, with myofibrillar synthesis about 20% higher in the first 4 hours and 40% higher from 4 to 12 hours; the authors report a negligible rise in amino acid oxidation.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The sample was 36 healthy, recreationally active young men tested once after a single resistance session, so these findings are not athlete data and may not apply to trained athletes, women or older adults. The study measures acute protein handling over 12 hours, not training adaptation, performance or injury outcomes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the title's 'no upper limit' as meaning larger protein doses always build more muscle, when only 0, 25 and 100 g were compared over 12 hours in healthy young men.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2023,
   "citation":"Trommelen J, van Lieshout GAA, Nyakayiru J, Holwerda AM, Smeets JSJ, Hendriks FK, et al. The anabolic response to protein ingestion during recovery from exercise has no upper limit in magnitude and duration in vivo in humans. Cell Rep Med. 2023;4:101324.",
   "doi":"10.1016/j.xcrm.2023.101324",
   "abstract":"Randomized, placebo-controlled tracer study in 36 healthy, recreationally active young men who ingested 0, 25 or 100 g of intrinsically labelled milk protein after a single bout of resistance exercise. The authors report that the magnitude and duration of the postprandial anabolic response, including plasma amino acid availability, muscle protein synthesis and whole-body protein balance, increased with the larger dose, while protein oxidation was barely affected.",
   "tldr":"A single 100 g protein dose after resistance exercise produced a larger and longer-lasting muscle protein synthesis response than 25 g in healthy young men. The study does not show that larger doses improve training outcomes, and it did not test athletes.",
   "methods":"Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in healthy, recreationally active men aged 18 to 40, with 12 per group ingesting 0, 25 or 100 g of intrinsically labelled milk protein after a whole-body resistance exercise session. A quadruple isotope tracer feeding-infusion approach with plasma and muscle biopsies was sampled over 12 hours to measure amino acid kinetics, whole-body protein synthesis and oxidation, and muscle protein synthesis.",
   "findings":"Plasma amino acid availability and tracer incorporation into muscle were higher after 100 g than 25 g over the 12-hour period. Myofibrillar protein synthesis (the primary outcome, based on the plasma leucine precursor) differed between all three doses, and was about 20% higher with 100 g than 25 g in the first 4 hours and about 40% higher from 4 to 12 hours. Whole-body protein synthesis increased with both protein doses, while the rise in amino acid oxidation was negligible in comparison.",
   "limitations":"The sample was 12 healthy, recreationally active men per group, tested after a single session, so the findings may not extend to trained athletes, women, older adults or clinical groups. Several responses had not returned to baseline by 12 hours, and tracer recycling means the rates are likely underestimates, so the authors describe their 100 g estimates as minimal. The title's claim of no upper limit rests on testing only three doses within one 12-hour window.",
   "practicalImplications":"A single 100 g protein dose gave a greater and longer muscle protein synthesis response than 25 g after resistance exercise in healthy young men, so the 20 to 25 g per meal guidance may not cap the acute response. The study does not show that such doses are needed, practical or better for athletes, or that meal size changes training gains.",
   "athleteDev":"The study measured acute protein synthesis after one session, not strength, muscle mass or performance gains, so it cannot show that larger post-training protein doses improve adaptation. It is best used to inform recovery nutrition discussions about meal protein size, pending evidence from trained athletes.",
   "rtp":"Participants were healthy, recreationally active men with no injury, so the study cannot inform nutrition for recovery from injury or return to sport. The authors note that clinically compromised or less active people may respond differently, which would also apply to injured athletes."
 }
}

          Abstract
          Matsuo, H, Funasaki, K, and Yamada, S. The applicability of the risk score approach to competitive sport: development of a physical
          success score for the Canadian football league combine. J Strength Cond Res 36(3): 695–701, 2022—In the scouting combine of
          the Canadian Football League (CFL), players are measured for 6 athletic abilities, including 2 measurements of body size. For
          coaches and their players who desire to play in the CFL, knowing the players metrics that are important for being drafted and their
          levels will help coaches plan and evaluate their training. Thus, the purpose of this study was to provide a simple scoring system using
          the predictors of CFL Combines identified by multivariate analysis and their regression coefficients, and reference values. In this
          study, authors created a scoring system to classify draft success and failure of CFL Combines based on the measurement results.
          This scoring system was named as the physical success score (PSS). To do so, a repeated grid-search cross-validation for variable
          selection algorithm was performed on the players (line: n 5 211, big skill linebacker, running back and tight end: n 5 177, skill
          [defensive back and wide receiver]: n 5 231) who participated in the CFL Combines between 2011 and 2019. The final binary
          logistic regression models and the reference values were used to generate the PSS for each group. As a result, PSS of the line, big
          skill, and skill were developed. In each group, all possible total scores and the estimated draft success probability were shown. From
          the results of this study, it was concluded that the PSS approach can provide useful information for coaches in setting training goals.
          Key Words: goal setting of training, multivariate analysis, scoring system

 "evidenceSummary":"A secondary analysis of public Canadian Football League Combine results from 2011 to 2019 for 221 line, 177 big-skill and 231 skill players, using logistic regression and a risk-score approach to build a physical success score (PSS) for each position group. Five-fold cross-validated validation AUCs were about 0.76 to 0.83 for the PSS, compared with 0.67 to 0.78 for a classification-tree benchmark, and the score tables show estimated draft-success probabilities that rise with total score (for example, 0.6% to 99.6% for the line group).",

   "doi":"",
   "abstract":"Secondary analysis of CFL Combine results from 2011 to 2019 for line, big-skill and skill players, using a repeated grid-search cross-validation procedure and logistic regression to build a physical success score (PSS) for each group. The authors report that the PSS gave better cross-validated prediction of draft success than a classification-tree benchmark and conclude that it can help coaches set training goals.",
   "tldr":"Using CFL Combine data from 2011 to 2019, the authors built simple physical success scores for linemen, big-skill and skill players, each linked to an estimated chance of being drafted. The score tables give coaches and players a practical set of body-size and athletic targets.",
   "methods":"Secondary analysis of publicly available CFL Combine results for 2011 to 2019, covering 221 line, 177 big-skill and 231 skill players, with drafting as a binary outcome. Candidate measures were height, weight, vertical jump, broad jump, bench press, 40-yard sprint, shuttle run and 3-cone drill. Variables were selected by repeated grid-search cross-validation, a final logistic regression was fitted for each group, and continuous measures were categorized by percentiles to build the score tables.",
   "findings":"Final models included height, weight, 40-yard sprint and vertical jump plus 3-cone drill for the line; height, weight, bench press, 40-yard sprint and 3-cone drill for big-skill players; and height, weight, bench press and 40-yard sprint for skill players. Validation AUCs for the PSS were about 0.77 (line), 0.76 (big skill) and 0.83 (skill), compared with 0.71, 0.67 and 0.78 for the classification-tree benchmark. The score tables map each total score to an estimated draft-success probability, for example from 0.6% to 99.6% for the line group.",
   "limitations":"Development and validation used the same public dataset, with no external validation and only 118, 68 and 88 selected players in the three groups. The outcome is draft selection, not later CFL performance, and the score covers combine measures only, not skill, game performance or injury. Some of the reported coefficient confidence intervals and AUC values are presented inconsistently in the text and tables, so the exact figures should be read with caution.",
   "practicalImplications":"Coaches and players aiming for the CFL can use the score tables to see the height, mass and athletic values linked to being drafted for each position group, and to set targets for sprint, jump and bench press work. The tables describe draft selection rather than skill, so they indicate a physical profile to work toward, not a complete standard.",
   "athleteDev":"The tables show which measures matter most for each position group, which can help prioritise strength and speed work, and how the total score changes with each measure. The model is based on draft outcomes, so it does not show that training a given measure will change a player's draft chances.",
   "rtp":"This study concerns draft selection of combine participants and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions."
 }
}

    The Association Between Alterations in Redox Homeostasis,
   Cortisol, and Commonly Used Objective and Subjective Markers
               of Fatigue in American Collegiate Football
            Benjamin A. McKay, Jace A. Delaney, Andrew Simpkin, Theresa Larkin, Andrew Murray,
                          Charlie Pedlar, Nathan A. Lewis, and John A. Sampson

     Purpose: To assess associations between a free oxygen radical test (FORT), free oxygen radical defense test (FORD), oxidative
     stress index, urinary cortisol, countermovement jump (CMJ), and subjective wellness in American college football. Methods:
     Twenty-three male student athlete American college football players were assessed over 10 weeks: off-season conditioning
     (3 wk), preseason camp (4 wk), and in season (3 wk). Assessments included a once-weekly FORT and FORD blood sample,
     urinary cortisol sample, CMJ assessment including ﬂight time, reactive strength index modiﬁed and concentric impulse, and a
     daily subjective wellness questionnaire. Linear mixed models analyzed the effect of a 2 within-subject SD change in the predictor
     variable on the dependent variable. The effects were interpreted using magnitude-based inference and are presented as
     standardized effect size (ES) ± 90% conﬁdence intervals. Results: Small negative associations were observed between
     FORT–ﬂight time, FORT–fatigue, FORT–soreness (ES range = −0.30 to −0.48), FORD–sleep (ES = 0.42 ± 0.29), and oxidative
     stress index soreness (ES = 0.56 ± 0.29). Small positive associations were observed between FORT–cortisol (ES = 0.36 ± 0.35),
     FORD–ﬂight time, FORD reactive strength index modiﬁed and FORD–soreness (0.37–0.41), oxidative stress index concentric
     impulse (ES = 0.37 ± 0.28), and with soreness–concentric impulse, soreness–ﬂight time, and soreness reactive strength index
     modiﬁed (0.33–0.59). Moderate positive associations were observed between cortisol–concentric impulse and cortisol–sleep
     (0.57–0.60). Conclusion: FORT/FORD was associated with CMJ variables and subjective wellness. Greater amounts of
     subjective soreness were associated with decreased CMJ performance, increased FORT and cortisol, and decreased FORD.

     Keywords: FORT/FORD, oxidative stress, countermovement jump, subjective wellness questionnaire, monitoring
